summary: Describes use cases for Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) that correspond to industry needs and that open interfaces and protocols would support. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes why one content delivery network might use another network's reach, capacity, or technical features. It also explains why content providers need their delivery policies to apply across the connected networks.

subtitle: Use cases for separate content delivery networks to extend reach, share capacity, or add capabilities.

tldr.problem: A standalone Content Delivery Network may lack the geographic reach, capacity, or delivery features requested by its customers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups CDN interconnection use cases into footprint extension, offload, and capability sharing, with delivery policies applying across participating networks.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC motivates CDNI interface requirements and obsoletes RFC 3570 to avoid confusion over terminology and models.

today: RFC 6770 is an Informational RFC and obsoletes RFC 3570. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 6770.

sections.title: Why CDNs Interconnect
sections.content:
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) can improve delivery experience and reduce costs for network operators and content providers. The RFC describes each CDN as a stand-alone network and presents CDN Interconnection (CDNI) as a way for connected CDNs to act together as a delivery infrastructure.

In the example, one CDN redirects a request to a partner CDN with a surrogate closer to the user. The content provider can make one business and technical arrangement with the first provider, while users may receive delivery from the partner. A content provider can also set limits on which partner may deliver its content.
sections.plainLanguage: One CDN can ask another CDN to deliver content where the second network has a suitable surrogate. The content provider's delivery rules still apply to the partner.

sections.title: Extending a CDN's Footprint
sections.content:
Footprint extension covers four cases: reaching additional geographic regions, connecting separate affiliates, having an ISP handle third-party content, and serving users who move between access networks. These cases let a provider reach locations or users beyond its own network.

An ISP can act as an Access CDN when it has surrogates in the same administrative network as the end user. A user away from a home ISP may receive the same content through a CDN in the network being used, subject to the content provider's policies.
sections.plainLanguage: CDNI can extend delivery to new regions, users on another network, or separate affiliates. The partner network may also provide a local cache for an ISP's subscribers.

sections.title: Offloading Traffic and Handling Failure
sections.content:
A CDN can offload requests when an unexpected traffic spike exceeds its expected peak or when it needs capacity for maintenance or an event. Providers with different peak periods may use each other's capacity, but the delivering CDN must be able to handle the requests it receives.

When delivery resources fail, a CDN can use internal recovery, send requests to the content provider's origin, or redirect requests to another CDN. For content acquisition, a CDN may switch between an origin and other sources. The acquisition protocols themselves are outside CDNI's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A CDN can send some requests to a partner during overload, maintenance, or failure. A CDN may also switch to another source when it cannot acquire content from its usual source.

sections.title: Sharing Delivery Capabilities
sections.content:
A CDN may interconnect with another provider when it lacks a delivery capability. The examples include support for HTTPS, delivery into mobile networks, or native IPv6 when the first CDN supports only IPv4 internally.

Interconnection can also support migration to new CDN technology, a multi-vendor strategy, or service-level requirements that the first provider cannot meet on its own. The partner CDN may have surrogates closer to the user or support a required delivery feature.
sections.plainLanguage: A CDN can use a partner when it lacks a protocol, network reach, or technology needed for a request. The partner delivers the content using the capability it provides.

sections.title: Content Delivery Policies Across CDNs
sections.content:
Content providers may set rules about when, how, and to whom a CDN delivers an asset. Examples include time windows, user-agent platform, resolution, authorization, access network, and geographic limits. These rules need to apply across interconnected upstream and downstream CDNs.

The delivery network does not need to understand the provider's business reason for a rule. The rule can be expressed as a check that each downstream CDN can enforce. The RFC focuses on use cases and does not analyze their threats; it points to RFC 6707 for that discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CDN in a delivery chain must enforce the content provider's delivery rules. The rules can be simple checks, such as verifying authorization or location.

viz.caption: THREE FAMILIES OF CDN INTERCONNECTION USE CASES

items.title: Footprint extension
items.text: Reach more regions, affiliates, or access networks.

items.title: Offload
items.text: Share capacity during overload, maintenance, or delivery failures.

items.title: Capability
items.text: Use a partner's delivery protocol, network, or technology.
